sectionTitle: Chemistry — Chemical measurements, conservation of mass and the quantitative interpretation of chemical equations

specStatements.text: The law of conservation of mass states that no atoms are lost or made during a chemical reaction so the mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants.
This means that chemical reactions can be represented by symbol equations which are balanced in terms of the numbers of atoms of each element involved on both sides of the equation.
Students should understand the use of the multipliers in equations in normal script before a formula and in subscript within a formula.
The relative formula mass ( M r ) of a compound is the sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms in the numbers shown in the formula.
In a balanced chemical equation, the sum of the relative formula masses of the reactants in the quantities shown equals the sum of the relative formula masses of the products in the quantities shown.
Students should be able to calculate the percentage by mass in a compound given the relative formula mass and the relative atomic masses.

Some reactions may appear to involve a change in mass but this can usually be explained because a reactant or product is a gas and its mass has not been taken into account. For example: when a metal reacts with oxygen the mass of the oxide produced is greater than the mass of the metal or in thermal decompositions of metal carbonates carbon dioxide is produced and escapes into the atmosphere leaving the metal oxide as the only solid product.

Students should be able to explain any observed changes in mass in non-enclosed systems during a chemical reaction given the balanced symbol equation for the reaction and explain these changes in terms of the particle model.
Whenever a measurement is made there is always some uncertainty about the result obtained.
represent the distribution of results and make estimations of uncertainty
use the range of a set of measurements about the mean as a measure of uncertainty.

scopeNotes.statement: given the relative formula mass and the relative atomic masses
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every percentage-by-mass item states the relative formula mass of the compound and the relative atomic masses it needs, exactly as the specification says these will be given. Students are never asked to recall or look up a relative atomic mass, and no item routes the calculation through moles or through masses in grams, because 4.3.1.2 asks only for a percentage worked from relative masses.

scopeNotes.statement: given the balanced symbol equation for the reaction
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Each item that asks for an explanation of an observed mass change supplies the balanced symbol equation in the stem, for example CuCO3 -> CuO + CO2. Students are never required to construct or balance the equation first in order to explain the change, and what is asked for is a particle-model explanation rather than a calculation.

scopeNotes.statement: use the range of a set of measurements about the mean as a measure of uncertainty
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Uncertainty is treated only as the spread of repeated measurements about their mean, quoted as the mean plus or minus half the range. No item asks for a standard deviation, a percentage uncertainty, or the combining of uncertainties through a calculation, none of which appear in 4.3.1.4.

scopeNotes.statement: balanced in terms of the numbers of atoms of each element involved on both sides of the equation
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Balancing is assessed as an atom count on each side and nothing more. No item uses fractional or half-integer coefficients, and none requires ionic or half equations, which belong elsewhere in the specification. Amount of substance in moles is not used anywhere in 4.3.1, so every quantitative item here stays in relative masses.

concepts.definition: The law of conservation of mass states that no atoms are lost or made during a chemical reaction so the mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants.
A representation of a reaction using chemical formulae, with the reactants on the left of the arrow and the products on the right.
A symbol equation in which the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides of the equation, which is what conservation of mass requires.
A number written in normal script before a formula, which multiplies every atom in that whole formula. In 2Ca(NO3)2 the leading 2 doubles the entire formula unit.
A small number written after a symbol, or after a closing bracket, which multiplies only the atom or the bracketed group that it immediately follows.
The relative mass of an atom of an element, the building block from which a relative formula mass is assembled.
The relative formula mass (Mr) of a compound is the sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms in the numbers shown in the formula.
In a balanced chemical equation the sum of the relative formula masses of the reactants in the quantities shown equals the sum of the relative formula masses of the products in the quantities shown.
The share of a compound's relative formula mass contributed by one element: the Ar of that element multiplied by the number of its atoms, divided by the Mr of the compound, then multiplied by 100.
A reaction vessel open to the surroundings, so a gaseous reactant can enter or a gaseous product can leave without being weighed on the balance.

concepts.term: Thermal decomposition of a metal carbonate
concepts.definition: Heating breaks the carbonate down into the metal oxide and carbon dioxide; the carbon dioxide escapes into the atmosphere, leaving the metal oxide as the only solid product.

concepts.term: Particle model explanation of a mass change
concepts.definition: An account of an apparent mass change in terms of gas particles entering the vessel from the air, or leaving it and dispersing among the particles of the air.
The doubt that always exists about the result of a measurement, present whenever a measurement is made, however good the apparatus and the technique.
The pattern formed by a set of repeated measurements, showing where the results cluster and which of them lie apart from the rest.
A measurement lying well outside the cluster formed by the others; it is spotted when the distribution is represented and is excluded from the mean.

concepts.term: Range as a measure of uncertainty
concepts.definition: The difference between the largest and the smallest of a set of measurements, used about the mean as a measure of uncertainty and quoted as the mean plus or minus half the range.

misconceptions.question: Marble chips and acid fizz in an open beaker and the balance reading falls by 0.8 g. Has mass been destroyed?
misconceptions.correct: No. The 0.8 g has left the beaker as carbon dioxide gas. Weigh the gas as well and the total is unchanged, because no atoms are lost or made.
misconceptions.misconception: In a chemical reaction atoms themselves can be created or destroyed, so the total mass of the substances can rise or fall.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students trust the balance over the law. A gas is invisible and disperses, so it stops feeling like a substance at all, and the falling reading looks like direct evidence that matter has disappeared.
misconceptions.correction: Ask where the atoms went, not where the mass went. Every carbon and oxygen atom in the escaping gas came from the marble and the acid and still exists; the balance simply no longer has them on it.

misconceptions.question: Does the law of conservation of mass hold in an open crucible?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The law holds in every chemical reaction. A sealed vessel only makes it easier to observe, because then nothing can enter or leave the balance pan.
misconceptions.misconception: Mass is only conserved when the reaction is carried out in a sealed container.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every classroom demonstration of constant mass uses a stopper or a sealed flask, so the seal gets remembered as a condition of the law rather than as a way of seeing it.
misconceptions.correction: Separate the law from the measurement. The seal changes what the balance can see, not what the atoms do; in an open vessel the atoms are all still there, just not all on the pan.

misconceptions.question: In 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, is the number of molecules the same on both sides?
misconceptions.correct: No. Three molecules become two. It is the number of atoms of each element that is unchanged: four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms on each side.
misconceptions.misconception: Mass is conserved because the number of molecules stays the same during a reaction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read a formula as a single unbreakable object and count formulae rather than atoms, so conservation gets attached to the wrong quantity.
misconceptions.correction: Count atoms element by element on each side. Molecules are taken apart and rebuilt during a reaction, so their number often changes; the atoms are only rearranged.

misconceptions.question: Does conservation of mass apply to chemical reactions as well as to melting and dissolving?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. It applies to chemical reactions too, because atoms are rearranged rather than lost or made.
misconceptions.misconception: Mass is conserved in physical changes such as melting, but a chemical reaction makes a new substance so the mass can change.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A physical change obviously keeps the same stuff, while a reaction produces something visibly different, which makes it feel as though the amount of matter has changed too.
misconceptions.correction: Track the atoms through the change. New substances are new arrangements of the same atoms, so the total mass is fixed in both kinds of change.

misconceptions.question: H2 + O2 -> H2O is not balanced. Is changing the water to H2O2 a valid way to balance it?
misconceptions.correct: No. H2O2 is hydrogen peroxide, a different substance. Balance it by writing 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, changing only the numbers in front.
misconceptions.misconception: An equation can be balanced by changing the subscripts inside a formula until the atom counts match.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Changing a subscript is the quickest way to make the counts agree, and students who see balancing as an arithmetic puzzle do not notice that they have changed the substance itself.
misconceptions.correction: Formulae are fixed by the substance and may never be altered. Only the multipliers written in normal script in front of a formula can be changed when balancing.

misconceptions.question: Must a balanced equation have the same number of formulae on each side of the arrow?
misconceptions.correct: No. Only the number of atoms of each element must match. In 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O three molecules on the left give two on the right, and the equation is still balanced.
misconceptions.misconception: Balancing means making the same number of molecules, or the same number of substances, appear on each side of the arrow.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word balance suggests two equal piles, and the most visible things in an equation are the formulae rather than the atoms inside them.
misconceptions.correction: Make a table of elements and count atoms on each side. That is the only quantity balancing has to equalise.

misconceptions.question: Can an equation be balanced by adding a spare atom to whichever side is short?
misconceptions.correct: No. Every atom must belong to a formula, and formulae come in whole units set by the multiplier written in front of them.
misconceptions.misconception: If one side is one atom short you can simply add that atom on to make the counts agree.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat the equation as a sum to be made to add up rather than as a description of real substances reacting.
misconceptions.correction: Ask what substance the extra atom would be. If it does not correspond to a real reactant or product it cannot be written; adjust the multipliers instead.

misconceptions.question: In 2Ca(NO3)2, what does the leading 2 multiply?
misconceptions.correct: The whole formula unit, so there are 2 calcium atoms, 4 nitrogen atoms and 12 oxygen atoms altogether.
misconceptions.misconception: The number in front only multiplies the first element written in the formula.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The number sits immediately next to the first symbol, so proximity suggests it belongs to that symbol alone, exactly as a subscript does.
misconceptions.correction: Read the leading number as an instruction to write the formula out that many times. Doing so makes it obvious that every atom in the unit is multiplied.

misconceptions.question: In Ca(NO3)2 and in Ca(OH)2, what does the subscript 2 outside the bracket do?
misconceptions.correct: It multiplies everything inside the bracket: 2 nitrogen and 6 oxygen atoms in Ca(NO3)2, and 2 oxygen and 2 hydrogen atoms in Ca(OH)2.
misconceptions.misconception: The subscript after a bracket multiplies only the symbol written immediately before it, not the whole group.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Elsewhere a subscript does apply only to the symbol it follows, so students carry that rule across without noticing that this one follows a closing bracket.
misconceptions.correction: Treat the bracket as one package. A subscript after a closing bracket applies to the whole package, not to the last symbol inside it.

misconceptions.question: Is the relative formula mass of Ca(OH)2 equal to 40 + 16 + 1?
misconceptions.correct: No. The bracket doubles both the oxygen and the hydrogen, so Mr = 40 + 2(16 + 1) = 74.
misconceptions.misconception: Relative formula mass is found by adding the relative atomic mass of each element in the formula once each.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read a formula as a list of ingredients rather than as a count of atoms, and the subscripts are small and easy to skip when copying numbers down.
misconceptions.correction: Write out the atom count first, element by element, before adding anything, then multiply each relative atomic mass by that count.

misconceptions.question: In Ca(OH)2, is the calcium doubled as well?
misconceptions.correct: No. The calcium sits outside the bracket, so the subscript does not reach it; only the O and the H inside are doubled.
misconceptions.misconception: The subscript after the bracket doubles every atom in the formula, so the calcium is doubled too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: It is the over-correction that follows once students have learned that a leading multiplier applies to everything, and the two kinds of number get merged.
misconceptions.correction: Compare the two positions directly. A number in normal script in front applies to the whole formula; a subscript applies only to what stands immediately before it.

misconceptions.question: The relative atomic mass of oxygen is 16. What is the relative formula mass of O2?
misconceptions.correct: 32, because the molecule contains two oxygen atoms and 2 x 16 = 32.
misconceptions.misconception: The relative formula mass of O2 is 16, because that is the relative atomic mass of oxygen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The element is called oxygen and has one number in the data table, so the subscript in the molecular formula is read as part of the name rather than as a count of atoms.
misconceptions.correction: Ask how many atoms are in the particle. Elements that exist as molecules, such as O2, H2 and Cl2, have a relative formula mass of twice their relative atomic mass.

misconceptions.question: For 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO, is the total relative formula mass of the products 40?
misconceptions.correct: No. There are two MgO units, so the product total is 2 x 40 = 80, matching (2 x 24) + 32 = 80 on the left.
misconceptions.misconception: When totalling relative formula masses across an equation you add up one of each formula and ignore the numbers written in front.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Relative formula mass is learned from single formulae, so students work out the Mr of MgO correctly and then stop, forgetting that the equation asks for the quantities shown.
misconceptions.correction: Multiply each Mr by the number in front of its formula before adding. The two totals then agree, which is the check that the equation is balanced.

misconceptions.question: NH4NO3 contains 2 nitrogen atoms out of 9 atoms in total. Is nitrogen therefore 22% by mass?
misconceptions.correct: No. Percentage by mass compares masses, not counts: (2 x 14) / 80 x 100 = 35%.
misconceptions.misconception: Percentage by mass is the number of atoms of that element divided by the total number of atoms.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Counting atoms is much easier than weighing them, and the word percentage suggests a share of a total number rather than a share of a total mass.
misconceptions.correction: Put the relative atomic masses in before dividing. Hydrogen atoms are numerous but light, so a count and a mass share give very different answers.

misconceptions.question: Nitrogen has Ar = 14 and NH4NO3 has Mr = 80. Is the percentage of nitrogen 14 / 80 x 100?
misconceptions.correct: No. There are two nitrogen atoms in the formula, so it is (2 x 14) / 80 x 100 = 35%.
misconceptions.misconception: Percentage by mass is the element's relative atomic mass and the compound's relative formula mass divided one by the other, ignoring how many atoms are present.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The remembered formula is Ar over Mr, and the step that multiplies by the number of atoms drops out because both numbers are handed to the student ready made.
misconceptions.correction: Count the atoms of that element in the formula first and write the multiplication down before dividing, even when the count turns out to be one.

misconceptions.question: Copper heated in an open crucible gains mass. Where has the extra mass come from?
misconceptions.correct: From oxygen in the air, which has combined with the copper to form copper oxide, so the oxide is heavier than the metal was.
misconceptions.misconception: The metal has absorbed heat energy from the flame, and that energy has added to its mass.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Heating is the only thing the student did, so it becomes the obvious cause, and energy is spoken about as something that goes into a substance and stays there.
misconceptions.correction: Write the equation: 2Cu + O2 -> 2CuO. The gain equals the mass of oxygen taken from the air, which can be predicted and then checked on the balance.

misconceptions.question: Copper carbonate is heated and the solid loses mass. Has some of it been destroyed?
misconceptions.correct: No. CuCO3 -> CuO + CO2. The carbon dioxide escapes into the atmosphere, leaving the copper oxide as the only solid product.
misconceptions.misconception: Strong heating burns some of the solid away, so that part of it no longer exists.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday burning appears to consume things, and the residue really is lighter, so destruction looks like a reasonable description of what has happened.
misconceptions.correction: Collect the gas and weigh it. Its mass accounts exactly for the loss, showing that the atoms have moved rather than gone.

misconceptions.question: A reaction in an open flask loses mass. Does that break the law of conservation of mass?
misconceptions.correct: No. The law holds; the flask simply is not enclosing everything, so a gaseous product has left the balance without being weighed.
misconceptions.misconception: In a non-enclosed system mass genuinely is not conserved, so the law only applies to closed systems.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The balance reading is treated as the total mass of the reaction rather than as the mass of whatever happens to be sitting on the pan.
misconceptions.correction: Define the system before judging the law. Include the escaped gas in the accounting and the total is unchanged.

misconceptions.question: Does carbon dioxide gas have mass?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. A cubic decimetre of carbon dioxide has a mass of about 1.8 g, and it is that mass the balance loses when the gas escapes.
misconceptions.misconception: Gases have no mass, or so little that they cannot account for a change on the balance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Gases are invisible, they rise away, and nothing in everyday experience makes them feel heavy, so weightlessness becomes the default assumption.
misconceptions.correction: Weigh a sealed flask before and after filling it with carbon dioxide, or weigh a filled gas syringe, to make the mass of a gas concrete.

misconceptions.question: When a solid decomposes and gas is released, is the solid left behind lighter because its particles have spread apart?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is lighter because particles have left it altogether, not because the particles remaining have moved further apart.
misconceptions.misconception: Particles spreading further apart makes a substance weigh less.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Density and mass are conflated, and the particle model is used to explain expansion far more often than it is used to explain mass.
misconceptions.correction: Separate spacing from number. Mass depends on how many particles are present and what they are, not on how far apart they sit.

misconceptions.question: A burette can be read to 0.05 cm3. Is a burette reading free from uncertainty?
misconceptions.correct: No. Whenever a measurement is made there is always some uncertainty about the result obtained; a finer scale reduces it but never removes it.
misconceptions.misconception: A precise instrument gives an exact value, so there is no uncertainty in the result.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A digital or finely graduated display presents a definite-looking number, and the extra decimal places read as extra certainty.
misconceptions.correction: Ask two students to read the same burette and compare their answers. The spread makes the residual uncertainty visible.

misconceptions.question: Does repeating a measurement three times remove the uncertainty?
misconceptions.correct: No. Repeats let you estimate the uncertainty from the spread of the results, but some uncertainty always remains.
misconceptions.misconception: Once a measurement has been repeated and a mean taken, the result is certain.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Repeating is taught as the fix for unreliable data, so it is remembered as something that removes the problem rather than as something that measures it.
misconceptions.correction: Use the repeats to quote a range about the mean. The answer improves and gains an uncertainty; it does not lose one.

misconceptions.question: If a student takes a reading carefully and makes no mistakes, is the result free from uncertainty?
misconceptions.correct: No. Uncertainty is not the same as a mistake. It is present in every measurement, even one taken perfectly.
misconceptions.misconception: Uncertainty only appears when the experimenter has done something wrong.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday speech uncertain suggests careless or unsure, so the word is heard as a criticism of the person rather than as a property of the measurement.
misconceptions.correction: Distinguish a mistake, which can be eliminated, from uncertainty, which is the unavoidable doubt about where the true value lies.

misconceptions.question: Five titres are 24.8, 25.0, 25.1, 25.0 and 27.4 cm3. Should all five go into the mean?
misconceptions.correct: No. Representing the distribution shows 27.4 lying well away from the cluster, so it is anomalous and is left out of the mean.
misconceptions.misconception: Every result that was measured must be included, because leaving one out is fixing the data.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Honesty about data is rightly stressed, and students hear excluding a point as cheating rather than as a judgement supported by the distribution itself.
misconceptions.correction: Report the anomaly and say why it was excluded. Identifying anomalies is part of representing the distribution, not a way of hiding it.

misconceptions.question: Readings run from 24.8 to 25.2 cm3 about a mean of 25.0 cm3. Is the uncertainty 0.4 cm3?
misconceptions.correct: The range is 0.4 cm3, and the uncertainty about the mean is half of that, so the result is 25.0 plus or minus 0.2 cm3.
misconceptions.misconception: The uncertainty is the whole range, so the result is 25.0 plus or minus 0.4 cm3.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The range is the quantity that actually gets calculated, so it is the number to hand, and the halving step is easy to drop when the range is used about the mean.
misconceptions.correction: Draw the mean with the highest and the lowest values either side of it. The mean sits in the middle, so it is only half the range away from each end.

misconceptions.question: Is an equation balanced so that the energy given out equals the energy taken in?
misconceptions.correct: No. Balancing is a count of atoms of each element on each side. Energy is conserved too, but that is not what the numbers in an equation record.
misconceptions.misconception: A symbol equation is balanced in order to make the energy on each side of the arrow equal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Conservation of mass and conservation of energy are taught close together and share the word conserved, so the reason for balancing gets attached to the wrong conserved quantity.
misconceptions.correction: Ask what the numbers in the equation actually count. They count atoms, and nothing in a symbol equation records energy at all.

misconceptions.question: The Ar of oxygen is 16. Is the Mr of O2 equal to 16 + 2?
misconceptions.correct: No. The subscript is a count of atoms, so it multiplies rather than adds: Mr = 2 x 16 = 32.
misconceptions.misconception: The subscript in a formula is added to the relative atomic mass when working out a relative formula mass.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Relative formula mass is introduced as a sum, so every number in sight gets added, and a small subscript looks like just another number to include in the total.
misconceptions.correction: Write the atom count in words first, for example two oxygen atoms, then write 2 x 16. The subscript never enters the sum as itself.

misconceptions.question: H2 + O2 -> H2O has too few oxygen atoms on the right. Does putting a 2 in front of O2 fix it?
misconceptions.correct: No. That makes the surplus worse. Balance it as 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O.
misconceptions.misconception: When an equation does not balance, increase the multiplier on the side that seems to need more of that element.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students act on the impression that one element is short without recounting both sides, and doubling the reactant containing it feels like the obvious repair.
misconceptions.correction: Recount both sides after every change. Balancing is iterative, and each new multiplier has to be checked against every element, not just the one being fixed.

mcqs.stem: Which statement gives the law of conservation of mass?

options.text: No atoms are lost or made, so the products have the same mass as the reactants.
options.rationale: This is the law as the specification states it: the atom count is fixed, so the total mass is fixed.

options.text: Mass stays the same only when the reaction is run inside a sealed vessel.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who remember the stoppered flask of the demonstration as a condition of the law rather than as a way of observing it.

options.text: The number of molecules is unchanged, so the total mass cannot change.
options.rationale: Picked by students who count formulae rather than atoms; molecule numbers often do change, as in 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O.

options.text: Mass is conserved when a solid melts but not when it reacts chemically.
options.rationale: Attractive because a physical change visibly keeps the same substance while a reaction produces something different.

mcqs.stem: 8.0 g of magnesium is burned in an open crucible and 13.3 g of magnesium oxide is left. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: The heat energy taken in during the burning has added 5.3 g to the solid.
options.rationale: Heating is the only thing the student did, so it becomes the obvious cause of the gain in mass.

options.text: 5.3 g of oxygen from the air has joined the magnesium in the crucible.
options.rationale: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO. The crucible is open, so oxygen enters and is weighed with the product: 13.3 - 8.0 = 5.3 g.

options.text: Extra magnesium atoms have been made, which is why the mass rose.
options.rationale: The mirror image of thinking mass is destroyed when a gas escapes: here a rising balance is read as atoms appearing.

options.text: The law of conservation of mass fails because the crucible is open.
options.rationale: Selected by students who treat the balance reading as the total mass of the reaction rather than of what sits on the pan.

mcqs.stem: A student writes H2 + O2 -> H2O and is told it is not balanced. Which change balances it correctly?

options.text: Change the product to H2O2 so that two oxygen atoms appear on the right.
options.rationale: The quickest way to make the counts agree, but H2O2 is hydrogen peroxide, a different substance altogether.

options.text: Write a 2 in front of O2 so that four oxygen atoms become available.
options.rationale: Acts on the impression that oxygen is short without recounting; it doubles the side that was already in surplus.

options.text: Write a 2 in front of H2 and a 2 in front of H2O, leaving O2 alone.
options.rationale: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O gives four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms on each side, changing only the multipliers.

options.text: Add one more oxygen atom to the right-hand side of the arrow.
options.rationale: Treats the equation as a sum to be made to add up; a lone atom does not correspond to any product.

mcqs.stem: Why must a symbol equation be balanced?

options.text: So that the same number of molecules appears on both sides of the arrow.
options.rationale: The word balance suggests two equal piles, and formulae are more visible than the atoms inside them.

options.text: So that the number of different substances shown matches on both sides.
options.rationale: A second form of the same error: counting the formulae written down rather than the atoms they contain.

options.text: So that the energy given out matches the energy taken in by the reaction.
options.rationale: Conflates conservation of mass with conservation of energy; both hold, but balancing is a count of atoms.

options.text: No atoms are lost or made, so each element has equal atoms per side.
options.rationale: Balancing is the direct consequence of conservation of mass, stated in terms of the numbers of atoms of each element.

mcqs.stem: In the formula 2Ca(NO3)2, what do the large 2 at the front and the small 2 after the bracket each do?

options.text: The front 2 shows two calcium atoms; the small 2 shows two nitrogen atoms.
options.rationale: Reads both numbers as belonging to the symbol nearest to them, which is true of neither of them.

options.text: The front 2 doubles the whole formula; the small 2 doubles the bracket only.
options.rationale: A multiplier in normal script applies to the entire formula unit; a subscript after a bracket applies to the bracketed group.

options.text: The front 2 doubles only the calcium; the small 2 doubles the oxygen.
options.rationale: Carries the ordinary subscript rule across to a bracket, so only the last symbol inside gets multiplied.

options.text: Both 2s multiply every atom, so each count in the formula is doubled twice.
options.rationale: The over-correction that follows once students learn that a leading multiplier applies to everything.

mcqs.stem: Calculate the relative formula mass of Ca(OH)2. Relative atomic masses: Ca = 40, O = 16, H = 1.

options.text: 57, from adding 40, 16 and 1 with the bracket subscript ignored.
options.rationale: Reads the formula as a list of ingredients, taking each relative atomic mass once.

options.text: 58, from doubling the hydrogen atoms but keeping one oxygen.
options.rationale: Applies the subscript to the symbol just before the closing bracket rather than to the whole group.

options.text: 74, because the bracket doubles both the oxygen and the hydrogen.
options.rationale: Mr = 40 + 2(16 + 1) = 40 + 34 = 74, the sum of the relative atomic masses in the numbers shown.

options.text: 114, from doubling every atom in the formula, the calcium included.
options.rationale: Treats the subscript as though it were a multiplier in normal script in front of the whole formula.

mcqs.stem: The relative atomic mass of oxygen is 16. What is the relative formula mass of O2?

options.text: 16, since that is the relative atomic mass given for oxygen.
options.rationale: The data table gives one number for oxygen, so the subscript is read as part of the name.

options.text: 16, since writing O2 does not add any mass to the oxygen.
options.rationale: Ignoring the subscript, the student keeps oxygen's Ar of 16 as the whole molecule's Mr (m12).

options.text: 18, from adding 16 to the 2 written in the formula.
options.rationale: Adds the subscript instead of using it as a count of atoms, a common slip under time pressure.

options.text: 32, because the molecule contains two atoms of oxygen.
options.rationale: Mr is the sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms in the numbers shown: 2 x 16 = 32.

mcqs.stem: For 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO the reactants total (2 x 24) + 32 = 80. The Mr of MgO is 40. What is the product total?

options.text: 80, since the same atoms are present on each side.
options.rationale: The quantity shown is 2MgO, so 2 x 40 = 80, equal to the reactant total as a balanced equation requires.

options.text: 40, because the relative formula mass of MgO is 40.
options.rationale: Works out the Mr of one formula correctly and then stops, ignoring the multiplier in front of it.

options.text: 64, because the 2 in front multiplies only the magnesium.
options.rationale: Applying the coefficient 2 to only the first element Mg: 2x24 + 16 = 64 (m08).

options.text: 48, because only the magnesium ends up in the solid.
options.rationale: Leaves the oxygen out of the product because a gas is not felt to contribute any mass.

mcqs.stem: Ammonium nitrate is NH4NO3, with Mr = 80. The relative atomic mass of nitrogen is 14. What is the percentage by mass of nitrogen?

options.text: 22%, from the 2 nitrogen atoms among the 9 atoms in the formula.
options.rationale: Compares counts rather than masses; hydrogen atoms are numerous here but very light.

options.text: 17.5%, from using the mass of only one of the nitrogen atoms.
options.rationale: Applies the remembered Ar over Mr without first counting the nitrogen atoms present.

options.text: 35%, because the two nitrogen atoms give 28 out of the total of 80.
options.rationale: (2 x 14) / 80 x 100 = 35%, using the relative formula mass and relative atomic mass supplied.

options.text: 70%, from doubling for the two nitrogen atoms a second time.
options.rationale: Corrects the missing multiplication and then applies it once more, giving twice the right answer.

mcqs.stem: Which method gives the percentage by mass of an element in a compound?

options.text: Divide the number of atoms of that element by the total atoms, then x 100.
options.rationale: A share of the atoms is not a share of the mass, because atoms of different elements weigh different amounts.

options.text: Divide the Mr of the compound by the Ar of that element, then x 100.
options.rationale: The division is inverted, which always gives an answer above 100% and should be spotted at once.

options.text: Divide the Ar of the element by the Mr of the compound, then x 100.
options.rationale: Works only where the compound holds a single atom of that element; the atom count is missing.

options.text: Multiply the Ar by the number of those atoms, divide by Mr, then x 100.
options.rationale: The standard route, using the relative formula mass and relative atomic masses the question supplies.

mcqs.stem: A weighed piece of copper is heated in an open crucible. The mass of the solid increases. Why?

options.text: Oxygen from the air has combined with the copper to form copper oxide.
options.rationale: 2Cu + O2 -> 2CuO. The oxide is heavier than the metal because the oxygen taken from the air is now weighed with it.

options.text: Heat energy absorbed from the flame has added to the mass of the metal.
options.rationale: Heating is the only visible input, and energy is spoken about as going into a substance and staying there.

options.text: The copper atoms expand as they get hot, so each one becomes much heavier.
options.rationale: Confuses a change in spacing or size with a change in mass, a very common particle-model slip.

options.text: New copper atoms are made as the reaction goes on in the crucible.
options.rationale: Reads a rising balance as atoms being created, the counterpart of reading a falling one as atoms destroyed.

mcqs.stem: Copper carbonate is heated in an open test tube: CuCO3 -> CuO + CO2. The mass of the solid falls. Why?

options.text: Some of the solid has been burned away by the heat of the Bunsen flame.
options.rationale: Everyday burning appears to consume things, and the residue really is lighter afterwards.

options.text: Carbon dioxide escapes, leaving copper oxide as the solid.
options.rationale: In the thermal decomposition of a metal carbonate the carbon dioxide escapes into the atmosphere, leaving the metal oxide as the only solid product.

options.text: Mass is lost from the tube, so mass is not conserved in this reaction.
options.rationale: Treats the balance reading as the total mass of the system rather than of what remains on the pan.

options.text: Strong heating has destroyed some of the solid, so that part no longer exists.
options.rationale: The solid is imagined to be burned away and to cease existing under strong heat (m17).

mcqs.stem: Use the particle model to explain why the balance reading falls when a metal carbonate is heated in an open tube.

options.text: The particles left in the tube move further apart, so the solid weighs less than before.
options.rationale: Explains a change in density rather than in mass; spacing does not alter how much matter is present.

options.text: Gas particles carry no mass of their own, so the reading falls as gas forms.
options.rationale: Gases are invisible and rise away, so weightlessness becomes the default assumption about them.

options.text: Particles are destroyed as the solid turns into a gas inside the hot tube.
options.rationale: Reads a change of state and substance as annihilation, which contradicts conservation of mass.

options.text: Carbon dioxide particles leave the tube and mix into the air, so they are no longer weighed.
options.rationale: The particle-model account the specification asks for: the particles still exist, but they are no longer inside the system on the balance.

mcqs.stem: A student reads 25.00 cm3 from a burette, working carefully. Which statement about that measurement is correct?

options.text: There is always some uncertainty about the result, however careful you are.
options.rationale: Whenever a measurement is made there is always some uncertainty about the result obtained.

options.text: There is no uncertainty, because a burette is precise apparatus.
options.rationale: A finely graduated scale looks definite, and the extra decimal places read as extra certainty.

options.text: Uncertainty appears only if the student misreads the burette scale.
options.rationale: Hears uncertain as careless, so uncertainty is treated as a fault rather than a property of measuring.

options.text: Uncertainty would disappear if the whole titration were repeated three times.
options.rationale: Repeating is taught as the fix for unreliable data, so it is remembered as removing the problem.

mcqs.stem: Five titres are 24.8, 25.0, 25.1, 25.0 and 27.4 cm3. How should this set of results be handled?

options.text: Include all five in the mean, because a measured result may never be dropped.
options.rationale: Honesty about data is rightly stressed, so excluding a point is heard as cheating.

options.text: Plot all five, treat 27.4 as anomalous and leave it out of the mean.
options.rationale: Representing the distribution shows 27.4 lying well away from the cluster, which is how an anomaly is identified.

options.text: Just take the mean and treat it as the exact result, since averaging removes any doubt.
options.rationale: Believing a mean is certain, the result is quoted as exact with no uncertainty (m22).

options.text: Use a single titre, since a precise burette gives the exact volume.
options.rationale: A precise instrument is thought to give an exact value, so one reading suffices (m21).

mcqs.stem: Four titres have a mean of 25.0 cm3, a lowest value of 24.8 cm3 and a highest of 25.2 cm3. How should the result be quoted?

options.text: 25.0 plus or minus 0.4 cm3, quoting the whole range as the uncertainty.
options.rationale: The range is the number to hand, and the halving step is easy to drop when using it about the mean.

options.text: Report all four titres separately, since no reading may be left out.
options.rationale: Insisting every reading be kept, the student lists all titres instead of a quoted result (m24).

options.text: 25.0 plus or minus 0.2 cm3, which is half the range of 0.4 cm3.
options.rationale: The range 25.2 - 24.8 = 0.4 cm3 is used about the mean, so the uncertainty quoted is half of it.

options.text: 25.0 cm3 exactly, since averaging the titres removes the uncertainty.
options.rationale: Taking a mean is believed to make the result certain, so it is quoted as exact (m22).
